Where Did Life Begin?

The oldest confirmed evidence of life on Earth comes from stromatolites — layered mats produced by microbial communities — found in rocks approximately 3,500 million years old (3,500 Ma). This tells us that life had already appeared within the first billion years of Earth’s history. How it began is one of the most actively researched questions in science, and two environments are considered the most plausible settings: hydrothermal pools on land, and deep-ocean black smokers on the seafloor.

Both settings share key features: they concentrate chemical compounds, supply energy (heat and chemical gradients), and could have provided the conditions for simple organic molecules to form and combine into more complex structures. The deep-ocean black smoker hypothesis has gained support because early Earth’s surface was subjected to intense ultraviolet radiation (there was no ozone layer yet), so deep-sea environments would have been more protected. Neither hypothesis has been conclusively proven, and the origin of life remains an open scientific question.

Key Fact

The oldest evidence of life on Earth is approximately 3,500 Ma old — preserved as stromatolites (layered microbial mats) in ancient rocks. This places the origin of life within the first billion years of Earth’s history, during the Archean eon.

From Single Cells to Complex Life

For the first two billion years after life appeared, it remained microscopic and single-celled. The first step up in complexity came with the appearance of cells containing a nucleus (eukaryotes) around 1,800 Ma, and the first multicellular organisms appeared around 600 Ma. The Phanerozoic eon, which begins at the Cambrian (541 Ma), is defined by the appearance of hard-bodied animals whose remains preserve well as fossils.

The Cambrian Explosion — a geologically rapid diversification of animal body plans — is spectacularly documented in the Burgess Shale of British Columbia, Canada (approximately 508 Ma). The Burgess Shale preserves soft-bodied organisms that would normally leave no trace, giving a rare window into the full range of Cambrian life. From this Cambrian foundation, the major animal lineages diversified through the Palaeozoic era (541–252 Ma): fish appeared in the Ordovician, amphibians colonised the land in the Devonian, reptiles first appeared in the Carboniferous and dominated the land by the Permian, and mammals and birds diverged from reptile lineages in the Mesozoic era.

Key Fact

The sequence of first appearances in the fossil record follows evolutionary complexity: fish (Ordovician), amphibians (Devonian), reptiles (Carboniferous), mammals (Triassic), birds (Jurassic). Mammals and birds both evolved from reptile lineages, not from each other. This sequence is the basis for cladograms in your exam.

Landmark Fossil Finds

Archaeopteryx, discovered in the Solnhofen Limestone of Germany in 1861, is one of the most famous fossils in science. Aged at approximately 150 Ma (Jurassic), it shows a combination of bird-like features (flight feathers) and reptilian features (teeth, clawed fingers, a long bony tail). It is considered a key transitional fossil showing the link between non-avian dinosaurs and modern birds.

Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis) is a partial skeleton discovered in Ethiopia in 1974, aged approximately 3.2 million years old. Her fossilised bones show features of both upright walking (the shape of her knee and pelvis) and tree-climbing (curved finger bones). Lucy is a crucial fossil in understanding the evolution of hominids — the group that includes modern humans and their immediate ancestors.

Mass Extinctions

The history of life is not one of steady progressive improvement — it is punctuated by catastrophic mass extinctions. There have been five major mass extinctions recognised in the Phanerozoic fossil record. The most severe was the end-Permian extinction (approximately 252 Ma), which wiped out an estimated 90 to 96% of marine species. The most famous is the Cretaceous-Palaeogene (K-Pg) extinction at approximately 66 Ma, which ended the non-avian dinosaurs and many other groups, clearing the ecological space for mammals to diversify.

The K-Pg extinction is supported by a global layer of iridium-rich clay found at the Cretaceous–Palaeogene boundary in rocks worldwide. Iridium is rare in Earth’s crust but abundant in meteorites, leading to the hypothesis (developed by Luis and Walter Alvarez in 1980) that a large asteroid impact contributed to the extinction event. Evidence for the impact includes the Chicxulub crater in Mexico (approximately 200 km in diameter), dated to approximately 66 Ma. Volcanic activity from the Deccan Traps in India at the same time also contributed to environmental disruption.

A cladogram is a branching diagram that shows evolutionary relationships. Each branch point (node) represents a common ancestor shared by the groups on either side of the split. In geology and palaeontology, cladograms are built using both fossil evidence (which body plan appeared first, which features are shared) and, for more recent organisms, molecular evidence (DNA comparisons).

A simple cladogram for vertebrates would place fish as the earliest branch, with amphibians diverging next (sharing the bony limb inherited from fish), then reptiles (adding the amniotic egg), then birds and mammals branching from reptile lineages. In the exam, you may be asked to read a cladogram — identify which group is most closely related to which, or use the cladogram to work out the order in which features evolved. The node is the key: groups that branch from the same node share a common ancestor and are more closely related than groups that share only a deeper node.

The fossil record is a biased sample of past life. Organisms with hard parts (shells, bones, teeth) are far more likely to be preserved than soft-bodied organisms, which is why the Burgess Shale is so exceptional — it shows us what we normally miss. Preservation requires rapid burial in sediment, which is more likely in marine and lake environments than on land. As a result, marine invertebrates are heavily over-represented in the fossil record compared to terrestrial vertebrates.

Even well-preserved organisms may never be found — they may be eroded away, buried too deeply, or simply never encountered by geologists. This means the fossil record always underestimates biodiversity and can never give a complete picture of ancient life. When a new fossil is found that extends the known range of a group earlier in time, it does not contradict evolution — it fills a gap that was always expected to exist. Examiners sometimes ask students to explain why the absence of a fossil in one rock unit does not prove that organism did not exist at that time.

This lesson covers general fieldwork skills required by the spec. Your school will have done specific fieldwork at a specific location — refer to your teacher's notes for your own examples and case-study data.

The Simplified Geological Map

Your written examination (the practical-skills component) is entirely based on a simplified geological map. Unlike the full 1:50,000 BGS maps used in professional work, the exam version uses a small number of named rock units, shows faults and fold axes clearly, and is accompanied by a cross-section framework and a stratigraphic column. The skills you need are: reading the map to identify rock types at any point, inferring structure from the map pattern, drawing or completing a cross-section, and constructing a sequence of geological events from the evidence shown.

Map reading is not passive. When you look at a simplified geological map, you should immediately ask: are the rock unit boundaries roughly parallel to the contours (horizontal strata), or do they cross contours (indicating dipping strata)? Are there any V-shaped bends in boundaries where a stream crosses them — and does the V point upstream (strata dipping upstream, or horizontal strata following the contours) or downstream (strata dipping downstream)? These V-patterns, combined with knowing the rule of Vs, allow you to infer the dip direction of strata before any other information is given.

Key Fact

The rule of Vs: when a geological boundary crosses a valley, the V points in the direction of dip. Horizontal strata follow the contours, so their V points upstream. Strata dipping upstream produce a V pointing upstream — sharper than the contour V. Strata dipping downstream produce a V pointing downstream. Vertical strata show no V at all — the boundary crosses the valley in a straight line.

Constructing a Cross-Section

A geological cross-section shows what the geology looks like on a vertical slice through the Earth along a given line on the map. To construct one:

First, draw the topographic profile — plot the elevation at each point where a contour crosses your section line, then join the dots with a smooth curve. Next, mark where each geological boundary crosses the section line at the surface. Use the dip angles and directions given on the map (shown as dip arrows with the angle written beside them) to project boundaries downward into the subsurface at the correct angle. In exam answers, show the beds as parallel lines within each rock unit, continuing the boundary angles consistently. Faults are drawn as straight lines cutting across bedding at the correct dip, with the displacement clearly shown.

Constructing a geological history from a map is one of the highest-tariff skills in the practical-skills component. The method uses three principles in sequence: superposition (older rocks are below younger ones in an undisturbed sequence), cross-cutting relationships (any feature that cuts across another is younger: a fault cutting through bedding formed after the bedding; a dyke intruding across a fault formed after the fault), and unconformities (a surface of erosion representing a gap in the geological record, with younger horizontal beds resting on older tilted beds). Exam technique: state the events in order from oldest to youngest, use the names of the specific rock units shown on the map, and state the principle of evidence for each step. Do not just describe what you see — you must explain how the evidence leads to the conclusion.

Graphic Logs

A graphic log (or sedimentary log) is a vertical column drawn to scale showing the rock types and thicknesses encountered in a borehole or at an outcrop. Each rock type uses a standard symbol: dots for sandstone, dashes for mudstone, brick-pattern for limestone, and so on. Additional columns to the right record grain size (coarsening-up or fining-up sequences), fossils found at each level, and sedimentary structures such as cross-bedding or ripple marks. Reading a graphic log allows you to reconstruct the environment of deposition — alternating sandstones and mudstones suggest a fluctuating energy environment such as a tidal flat or delta margin; a thick uninterrupted limestone suggests a stable shallow marine environment.

In the field, a compass clinometer measures the dip angle and strike direction of rock surfaces such as bedding planes or fault planes. Strike is the compass direction of a horizontal line on the surface; dip is the maximum angle of inclination, measured perpendicular to strike. These values are plotted as dip arrows on a geological map. GPS is used to record the precise location of observations, ensuring measurements can be placed accurately on the map.

A rose diagram is a circular graph used to display directional data — for example, the strike directions of joints measured across an outcrop, or the orientation of pebble long-axes in a conglomerate. Petals on the rose represent the frequency of measurements in each compass direction. A rose diagram with two opposite petals suggests a single dominant joint set; one with four petals suggests two conjugate joint sets related to a tectonic stress field. In your exam, you may be asked to read a rose diagram and describe the dominant trend, or to explain what the pattern reveals about past stress or current flow directions.

Rock description in the field uses standardised language: for igneous rocks — colour, grain size (fine/medium/coarse), texture (porphyritic, vesicular, glassy), mineralogy (quartz, feldspar, mica as visible crystals). For sedimentary rocks — grain size, sorting, rounding, colour, sedimentary structures, fossil content. For metamorphic rocks — foliation (slate, schist) or banding (gneiss, but note gneiss is not on the spec; if in doubt, describe the texture without naming). Using only rock names that appear on the specification is essential for exam marks.

The Fieldwork Statement and Directed Investigation

The specification requires two field occasions before the exam, at least one of which must be a directed investigation — where you formulate a question, collect data systematically, and interpret your findings. There is no submitted portfolio; the fieldwork prepares you for examination questions that ask about field methods, data collection and interpretation. You may be asked to describe how you would carry out a field survey, what equipment you would use, how you would record data (field sketches, annotated drawings, written descriptions, graphic logs), and how you would process and present it (rose diagrams, cross-sections, geological histories).

Key Fact

Key fieldwork recording methods: field sketch (hand-drawn panoramic view of an outcrop with annotations for rock types, structures and features); annotated photograph (scaled photograph with labels identifying geological features); graphic log (scaled vertical column showing rock sequence and thicknesses); rose diagram (circular frequency plot of directional data). Each serves a different purpose and examiners may ask you to select and justify the most appropriate method for a given task.

The Geological Code of Conduct

All geological fieldwork in the UK is guided by The Geological Code of Conduct. Key principles include: always seeking permission from landowners before entering private land; working safely — never hammering at the base of an unstable face; collecting specimens minimally and only where legal; respecting other users of the countryside; and reporting significant new finds to geological bodies or local record centres. In your exam, if asked about responsible fieldwork, cover permission, safety and minimal impact.
